Review: Units 01–08

Unit 1.1

Introducing yourself

Use I am (short form I'm) and your name to introduce yourself. My name is works the same way. To introduce another person, say This is for one person, or These are for more than one. You can add His name is or Her name is too.

Hi, I'm Diego. My name is Priya. This is my friend, Noah. Her name is Ms. Alvarez. She is our teacher.

Subject + to be

Subjectto beContraction
IamI'm
YouareYou're
HeisHe's
SheisShe's
ItisIt's
WeareWe're
TheyareThey're

We often use the short form in speech, like "I'm Marco." The full form, like "I am Marco," sounds a little more formal.

Grammar practice: complete each introduction

  1. You stand up in a new class. Hello, everyone! Sofia.
  2. A formal introduction Nadia. I am your teacher today.
  3. A casual introduction, at a party Hi, Marco.
  4. Introducing a classmate This is my classmate. Ben.
  5. Introducing your cousins These are my cousins. Mia and Zoe.
  6. Checking someone's name Ms. Alvarez, right? Nice to meet you.
  7. Introducing yourself and a friend Nice to meet you! Aiko and Kenji.
  8. Introducing your teacher This is our teacher. Mrs. Owens.

Reading practice

It is the first day of summer school. The teacher asks each student to stand up. "I'm Aiko," says a girl. "This is my friend, Kenji. We're from Osaka." The teacher smiles. "My name is Ms. Alvarez. I'm your teacher this summer." Next, a tall boy stands up. "Good morning! My name is Diego." A quiet girl speaks last. "I am Priya. This is my roommate, Noor. Her name is a little hard to say, but that's OK!" Everyone laughs. "Great!" says Ms. Alvarez. "Now we're all friends. Let's start."

Check your understanding

1. Aiko and Kenji are from the same city.

2. Ms. Alvarez is a new student.

3. Diego uses "My name is" to introduce himself.

4. Priya's roommate is named Noor.

5. This is the last day of school.

Unit 3.1

How old are you?

Say your age with a subject, a form of to be, a number, and years old. Ask about someone's age with How old is/are...? We often drop "years old" in speech. "I'm 29" is the same as "I'm 29 years old."

I'm 27 years old. How old is your grandfather? We're both 19. They're turning 40 next month.

Subject + to be + years old

Subjectto beExample
IamI'm 29 years old.
YouareYou're 22 years old.
He / She / ItisShe's 8 years old.
We / TheyareThey're 70 years old.

In questions, "is" or "are" comes before the subject. We say "How old is she?" We do not say "How old she is?"

Grammar practice: complete each sentence

  1. Liam just had his birthday. 11 years old.
  2. Talking about yourself 29 years old.
  3. Your grandparents are the same age. both 70 years old.
  4. Asking a friend her age So, are you now?
  5. Talking about a new kitten only 2 months old.
  6. You and a friend are the same age. both 22.
  7. Sara's little sister only 8 years old.
  8. Your new boss looks young. only 45? You look young!

Reading practice

"I'm 80 today," she laughs, "but I still feel 30!" Her granddaughters, Elena and Rosa, are twins. "We're 16," says Elena. "Next year we'll be 17." Uncle Carlos has a new puppy. "He's only three months old," Carlos says, "but he already thinks he owns the farm!" Grandma looks at her whole family. "You're all growing up so fast," she says.

Check your understanding

2. Mateo is Grandma's youngest grandchild.

3. Elena and Rosa are the same age.

4. Carlos's puppy is more than one year old.

5. The family meets every summer.

Unit 5.1

Possessive adjectives

A possessive adjective comes before a noun. It shows who something belongs to: my, your, his, her, its, our, their. These words do not change. We use her for both "her book" and "her books."

Max is my dog. Is that your bike? Nina lost her keys. The company changed its logo.

Subject pronoun → possessive adjective

SubjectPossessive adjectiveExample
Imymy dog
Youyouryour bike
Hehishis book
Sheherher keys
Ititsits tail
Weourour house
Theytheirtheir toys

Do not confuse its (possessive, no apostrophe) with it's ("it is"). Use whose to ask about possession: "Whose keys are these?" "They're Nina's."

Grammar practice: choose the right word

  1. (I) Max is dog. He loves the park.
  2. (you) Is this jacket on the chair?
  3. (she) Priya lost umbrella again.
  4. (they) The players lost first game this season.
  5. (it) The company changed website last month.
  6. (he) Omar can't find glasses.
  7. (we) flight leaves at noon.
  8. Asking about ownership backpack is this?

Nearby, two brothers, Sam and Alex, look at a water bottle. "Whose bottle is this?" Sam asks. "It's mine," says Alex. The other coach checks his notes and reads out their names for tonight's game. "Remember," says Coach Ramirez, "our goal is not just to win. It's to play our best."

Check your understanding

1. The team got new shirts.

2. Omar forgot his shoes.

3. The water bottle belongs to Alex.

4. Coach Ramirez is the other coach.

5. Winning is the team's only goal.

Units 6.1, 6.5

Apostrophe with 's

Add 's to a singular noun to show possession. If a plural noun already ends in -s, add only an apostrophe. Some plural words, like children and men, do not end in -s. We still add 's to these words. For a name that ends in -s, like James, we can write James's or James'. When two people own one thing together, only the second name gets 's: Tom and Rosa's car.

Ana's brother is a doctor. My parents' car is red. The children's shoes are new. James's office is on the third floor.

Forming the possessive

Noun typeRuleExample
Singular nounadd 'sAna's brother
Plural noun ending in -sadd ' onlymy parents' car
Irregular plural (no -s)add 'sthe children's shoes
Singular name ending in -sadd 's (or ')James's office

Grammar practice: pick the correctly formed possessive

  2. more than one girl, their bags
  3. Ana, her mother
  4. the children, their toys
  5. one teacher, her desk
  6. more than one boy, their bikes
  7. the men, their coats (irregular plural)
  8. Tom and Rosa share one car together

Units 5.6, 8.1

This, that, these, those

This and that point to one thing. These and those point to more than one. This and these are for things close to you. That and those are for things far away. These words can also stand alone, without a noun after them: "I love this!"

This is my phone. That is your phone. These are my keys, and those are yours. I love this song.

Near / far × singular / plural

NearFar
Singularthisthat
Pluralthesethose

These words work with or without a noun: "This bag is mine" and "This is mine" are both correct.

Grammar practice: choose the right word

  1. You hold one umbrella. is my new umbrella.
  2. You see a house far down the road. is where my aunt lives.
  3. You hold two notebooks. are my notes.
  4. You see mountains far away. are the Andes.
  5. You hold one shell you just found. is the biggest shell I have found.
  6. You hold five letters. need to go in the mail today.
  7. You point at a painting across the room. painting is worth a lot.
  8. You point at stars high in the night sky. are actually planets, not stars.

Woman: Excuse me, how much are these apples?

Man: These red apples are two dollars a bag. Those green apples over there are three dollars.

Woman: I'll take this bag, please. And what's that?

Man: That's honey from my farm. It's very good.

Woman: Are these jars small or large?

Man: These are small. Those on the top shelf are large.

Woman: I'll take one of those large jars, please.

Unit 8.7

Determiners and pronouns

A possessive adjective comes before a noun, like my keys. A possessive pronoun stands alone and replaces the noun, like they're mine. Possessive pronouns never have an apostrophe. We write hers, yours, theirs, ours. We do not write her's or your's.

These are my shoes. Those shoes are mine. Is this your umbrella? Yes, it's yours. That desk is hers, not his.

Possessive adjective vs. possessive pronoun

Adjective (+ noun)Pronoun (alone)
mymine
youryours
hishis
herhers
ourours
theirtheirs

His is the same word in both columns: "his keys" and "they're his."

Grammar practice: adjective or pronoun?

  1. before a noun These are shoes.
  2. no noun after Those shoes are .
  3. before a noun Is this car?
  4. no noun after This car is .
  5. before a noun That is backpack.
  6. no noun after This backpack is .
  7. before a noun These are tickets.
  8. no noun after Those tickets are .
  9. before a noun That is apartment on the fifth floor.
  10. no noun after That apartment is .
  11. before a noun This is jacket, I think.
  12. no noun after That jacket on the hook is .

Reading practice

At the airport, people look for their bags. "Is this yours?" a man asks a woman, holding up a green suitcase. "No, that's not mine," she says. "Mine has a yellow ribbon on it." Nearby, two brothers, Leo and Sam, both grab the same backpack. "That's mine!" says Leo. "No, I think it's his," says Sam, pointing at a stranger. The stranger checks his own bag and laughs. "You're right, this is mine." A family finds four red suitcases. "These are ours," says the father, counting them again. Leo looks at his empty hands. "I think this backpack really was mine after all."

Check your understanding

1. The woman's suitcase has a yellow ribbon on it.

2. The green suitcase belongs to the woman.

3. The backpack belongs to the stranger.

4. The family has four matching suitcases.

5. Sam keeps the backpack.

Units 01–08

Speaking practice

Practice speaking like in a speaking exam such as IELTS. Part 1: answer short questions about you. Part 2: prepare for one minute, then talk about a topic for one to two minutes. Part 3: act out a conversation with a partner. Try first, then open the examples.

Part 1: Interview

Answer each question in one to three sentences. Don't just say "yes" or "no" — add a reason or an extra detail.

Introductions

1. What's your name? Can you spell it?

Show example answer
My name is Ana Souza. That's A-N-A, Ana, and S-O-U-Z-A, Souza.
Introductions

2. Where are you from?

Show example answer
I'm from Brazil. I'm from Recife. It's a big city in the northeast.
Age

3. How old are you?

Show example answer
I'm twenty-four years old. My birthday is in March.
Age

4. How old are the people in your family?

Show example answer
My mom is fifty-two, and my dad is fifty-five. My sister is nineteen, and my grandmother is eighty!
Possessive adjectives

5. Tell me about your best friend.

Show example answer
My best friend's name is Julia. Her birthday is in May, and her favorite color is green. Her dog's name is Bob.
Apostrophe 's

6. Whose phone is the newest in your family?

Show example answer
My sister's phone is the newest. My parents' phones are very old!
This / that / these / those

7. Look around the room. What is this? What is that?

Show example answer
This is my notebook, and these are my pens. That is the door, and those are the windows.
Pronouns

8. Your teacher holds up a pen. Is it yours?

Show example answer
No, it isn't mine. Mine is blue. I think it's hers. It's Maria's pen.

Part 2: Long turn

You have one minute to prepare. You can write some notes. Then talk for one to two minutes.

Describe a person in your family.

You should say:

  • who this person is
  • how old he or she is
  • what his or her name is and where he or she is from

and explain why you like this person.

0:00 Press a button to start
Show example answer
I want to talk about my brother. His name is Lucas, and he's twenty-eight years old. He's from São Paulo, like me, but now he lives in Curitiba. Lucas is a teacher. His students love him because he's very funny. His wife's name is Carla. She's thirty, and she's a nurse. Their son is my nephew, Theo. He's only two years old! I like my brother because he's kind and he always helps me. This is his favorite photo of us. In the photo, we're at our grandparents' house.

Part 3: Role-plays

Work with a partner. Student A and Student B read only their own card. Then have the conversation.

Meeting a new classmate

It's the first day of English class. Student A and Student B are new students.

Student A

  • Say hello and introduce yourself.
  • Say where you're from.
  • Ask B's age.
  • Introduce your friend (use an imaginary name).

Student B

  • Say hello and introduce yourself.
  • Answer A's questions.
  • Ask where A's friend is from.
  • Say how old you are.
Useful languageHi, I'm…Nice to meet you.Where are you from?How old are you?This is my friend…His / Her name is…
Show example dialogue

A: Hi! I'm Pedro. Nice to meet you.

B: Hi, Pedro. I'm Sofia. Nice to meet you, too.

A: Where are you from, Sofia?

B: I'm from Chile. And you?

A: I'm from Brazil. How old are you?

B: I'm twenty-two. How old are you?

A: I'm twenty-five. Oh, this is my friend. His name is Kenji.

B: Hi, Kenji! Where are you from?

A: He's from Japan. He's in our class, too.

B: Great! Welcome to the class!

At the lost and found

Student A works at the school's lost and found. Student B lost a bag.

Student A

  • Ask B what he or she lost.
  • Show B some bags: "Is this your bag?" "Are these your keys?"
  • Ask what B's bag looks like.
  • Give B the correct bag.

Student B

  • Say you lost your bag and your keys.
  • Answer A's questions: "No, that isn't mine." "Yes, those are mine!"
  • Describe your bag.
  • Say thank you.
Useful languageIs this yours?No, it isn't mine.Mine is…Are these your keys?Whose bag is that?That's my bag!
Show example dialogue

A: Hello. Can I help you?

B: Yes, please. I lost my bag and my keys.

A: Is this your bag?

B: No, that isn't mine. Mine is black.

A: What about that black bag over there?

B: Yes! That's my bag. Thank you!

A: And are these your keys?

B: No, those aren't mine. My keys are on a red key ring.

A: Oh, these keys have a red key ring. Are they yours?

B: Yes, they're mine. Thank you so much!

Writing practice

Read the task, plan your ideas, and write your text in the box. The counter shows how many words you have — it turns green when you're in the right range. Use the grammar from these units. When you finish, compare your text with the example.

Task 1: My student profile

Profile30–50 words

Your new English school wants a short profile of every student. Write about yourself.

Write about

  • your name and where you're from
  • your age
  • one person in your family (name and age)
  • your best friend and his or her favorite thing

Try to use

  • I'm… / My name is…
  • my / his / her / their
  • 's (my sister's name, Ana's birthday)
0 words
Show example text (37 words)
Hello! My name is Ana, and I'm from Brazil. I'm twenty-four years old. My sister's name is Bia. She's nineteen. My best friend is Julia. Her favorite thing is her bike. It's red and very fast!

Task 2: An email to a new pen pal

Email60–80 words

You have a new pen pal in the United States. Write an email and send a photo of your family. Describe the people in the photo.

Write about

  • introduce yourself
  • say who the people in the photo are (This is… These are…)
  • say how old they are
  • write about one thing that belongs to someone (my dad's car, our dog)

Try to use

  • This is / These are
  • possessive adjectives (my, his, her, our, their)
  • 's and s' (my parents' house)
  • mine / yours / theirs
0 words
Show example text (69 words)
Hi Emma, My name is Diego, and I'm from Mexico. I'm twenty years old. This is a photo of my family. This is my mom. She's forty-eight, and her name is Rosa. These are my brothers, Leo and Tomas. They're twins, and they're fifteen. That small white dog is ours. His name is Toto. The big house is my grandparents' house. What about your family? Best wishes, Diego
